questions.problem: Find the area of the rectangle $ABCD$ if its perimeter is $36$ and $BC=10.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the length of $AB$ by using the formula for the perimeter, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+CD+DA \\ p & =2AB+2BC \\ 36 & =2AB+2(10) \\ 36 & =2AB+20 \\ 2AB & =16 \\ AB & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the rectangle $ABCD$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =AB\cdot BC \\  & =10\cdot 8 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The perimeter of the rectangle $ABCD$ is $32.$ If $AB=3BC,$ then its area is $A=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $BC=x.$

Since the perimeter of the rectangle is $p=32$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+CD+DA \\ p & =2(AB)+2(BC) \\ 32 & =2(3x)+2(x) \\ 32 & =6x+2x \\ 8x & =32 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain $BC=4$ and $AB=3\cdot 4=12.$

Therefore, the area of a rectangle $ABCD$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =AB\cdot BC \\  & =12\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **area** of a shape is a measure of how much space is enclosed by a shape on a plane. Let's consider a square with sides of length of $1\,\textrm{in}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14195146/assets/bc59b6e5a60a2f22e6c7fb102eba2f255dd09e115fd04a16050570f9f8b053f4.png)

The area of this square is equal to ${\color{red}{1\,\textrm{in}^2}},$ which we say in words as "one square inch."

Similarly, if we have three squares with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm},$ $1\,\textrm{m},$ and $1\,\textrm{ft}$ respectively, then their respective areas will be 

$$
1\,\textrm{cm}^2, \qquad
	1\,\textrm{m}^2, \qquad 
	1\,\textrm{ft}^2.
$$

tutorials.name: The Area of a Square
tutorials.problem:
Let's now suppose that we would like to compute the area of the square $ABCD,$ shown below. Notice that, this time, the sides of the square span multiple unit lengths.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14195146/assets/1441893036f9a41ed0daa8c8ce078d6a733bab5bb88dc60259a6b9ebc1c2e7c0.png)

The length of one side of a grid square is equal to $1\,\textrm{cm}.$ So, the area of one grid square is $1\,\textrm{cm}^2.$ 

Now, we need to find how many grid squares are contained inside $ABCD.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14195146/assets/5f293762b05013689996298a7804fb5f507eb228112397641fb8f662ff74ba49.png)

Inside the large blue square, there are $3$ rows containing $3$ grid squares each, so we can fit exactly $3 \times 3 = 3^2 = 9$ grid squares inside $ABCD.$

Each grid square has area $1\,\textrm{cm}^2,$ so the area $\mathcal A$ of $ABCD$ is 

$$
\mathcal{A} = (3\,\textrm{cm})^2 = 9\,\textrm{cm}^2.
$$

In general, if we have a square with a side of length $a$, then the area of the square is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a^2.
$$

tutorials.name: The Area of a Rectangle
tutorials.problem:
In general, for a rectangle with sides of length $a$ and $b,$ the area of the rectangle is given by

$$
\mathcal{A} = a \cdot b.
$$

Let's demonstrate by finding the area of the rectangle $PQRS,$ shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14195146/assets/a0890441b4c7e888ca7ede71a075825ca6700f79d242d1dec7e35ab2d787e5e0.png)

From the figure, we see that the rectangle has the following side lengths:

$$
a = {PQ} = 10\,\mathrm{cm},
	\qquad
	b = {PS} = 6\,\mathrm{cm}.
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =a\cdot b \\  & =10\,\text{cm}\cdot 6\,\text{cm} \\  & =60\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

It does not matter which side we call $a$ and which side we call $b.$ In the above example, if we set

$$
a = {QR} = 6\,\mathrm{cm},
\qquad
b = {RS} = 10\,\mathrm{cm},
$$

 

then we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =a\cdot b \\  & =10\,\text{cm}\cdot 6\,\text{cm} \\  & =60\,{\text{cm}}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

as before.
